newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA MEDIA REFORM NOT SEEN FOR ANOTHER WEEK.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA MEDIA REFORM NOT SEEN FOR ANOTHER WEEK.

text.p: The Australian government was unlikely to announce proposed changes to the country's cross-media ownership laws for at least another week, a government official said on Tuesday.
"There is no announcement today and I'd be surprised if there was any announcement even after next week's cabinet meeting," the official told Reuters.
He said cabinet had discussed the issue on Tuesday, but ministers had to consult with the backbench committee on communications before any announcement was made.
"The matter of media ownership reform was discussed and further consultation will now occur with the backbench," the official said.

"Their intention is quite clear -- they want to talk to the backbench about it and until they have a chance to actually discuss it with their backbench colleagues, they're not intending to say anything else."
Under the current cross-media ownership laws, television station owners are banned from holding more than 15 percent of a newspaper in the same major market, and vice versa.
The Liberal-National government ordered a review of these limits soon after winning office in March 1996.

Media analysts have been alert to any signals that the government may be about to change media policy as it could affect the ownership of newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd and Seven Network Ltd.

Media barons Kerry Packer, who controls Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, and Rupert Murdoch, the executive chairman of global media group News Corp Ltd, have lobbied Prime Minister John Howard in recent months about the proposed changes.
Packer's PBL has about 15 percent of Fairfax, behind the 22 percent held by Brierley Investments Ltd of New Zealand, and has said it wanted to merge with Fairfax.
Murdoch has a 14 percent stake in Seven, the second ranked television group behind Packer's Nine Network, and has talked about raising the stake.
Murdoch's newspaper interests in Australia account for more than 60 percent of circulation in the major capital cities.
